extracted.intended_audience: Mathematicians preparing to write and submit articles to the AMS Notices (prospective Notices authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for preparing and submitting different types of articles to the AMS Notices, covering audience, structure, tone, length, reference limits, and type-specific expectations. Targets authors who want to communicate mathematical topics to the broad AMS membership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience — general AMS membership
rubrics_metrics.description: You are writing for the general AMS membership, which is broader than you might think. Your audience is not colleagues who work in your field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hook the non-specialists by making your article comprehensible and compelling. Target the introduction to mathematicians who have never taken a graduate course in your specialty. Write at a level intelligible to the general AMS member for at least the first couple pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction goals — answer core questions early
rubrics_metrics.description: The first few paragraphs of your article should achieve two goals: leave readers who stop after the introduction with answers to: What is your article about? Where is your subject coming from, where is it now, and where might it be going? Why is your topic interesting and exciting? And convince the reader to continue past the introduction and get into the heart of your article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sell your topic early: many readers will not read past the introduction, so provide the 'sizzle' up front.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't bury the punchline; adopt a journalistic structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Think more 'newspaper article' and less 'murder mystery.' The majority of your readers will not read to the end, so do not hide your punchline there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the most engaging parts of your story in the introduction even if technical details come later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and revision
rubrics_metrics.description: Some key principles for you as an author: Know what you want to say. Understand your audience. Think and write clearly. Repeatedly read and polish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading aloud often helps improve readability, especially for complicated sentences or paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid jargon and exclusionary phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using jargon that is familiar to people in your field, but is not standard terminology for the general mathematical community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid phrases such as 'Recall that X' or 'It is well known that X' or 'Clearly X is true,' since they signal to a reader unfamiliar with X that there is little hope of understanding the rest of the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: General reference ceiling
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles should include no more than 20 references that guide the reader to the literature, although with prior permission of the editor, survey articles may have a more comprehensive bibliography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many article types reiterate the 'no more than 20 references' rule; excess references require editorial permission and justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research Feature Articles — accessibility and length
rubrics_metrics.description: Research feature articles should include an appropriate level of detail to be largely comprehensible to most AMS members. It is especially important to start gently for the non-specialists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target length is 8–12 pages, with 15 pages an absolute upper limit. Include no more than 20 references (exceptions for surveys with editor permission). Ensure at least the first couple pages are intelligible to general AMS members (roughly mathematicians who have not taken a graduate course in your specialty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Community Feature Articles — tone and length
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles concerning professional and social issues should be of interest to a substantial fraction of the AMS membership and should be written in a scholarly tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is inappropriate to use inflammatory language, sweeping generalizations unsupported by evidence, or personal attacks; well-argued and respectfully presented opinions on important issues are welcome. Target length 8–12 pages, 15 pages absolute maximum, and no more than 20 references without editor permission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education Articles — scope and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Education articles include research on educational methods, policy, and outcomes, descriptions of innovative educational techniques, and reports/analyses that impact mathematical learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target length is 5–10 pages. Generally no more than 20 references; any excess needs justification and editor permission.

rubrics_metrics.name: "What Is...?" Articles — brevity and focus
rubrics_metrics.description: "What is…?" articles aim to briefly explain important mathematical concepts or topics to a broad mathematical audience. Clarity, an engaging presentation, and a sharp focus on conveying the significance of the subject matter are essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for the shortest path to answer 'What is X?' and 'Why is X interesting?'. Recommended length is 2–4 pages with a very short list of references, preferably at most 5.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book Reviews — format and length
rubrics_metrics.description: The Notices has a one-page Bookshelf Column where each month an associate editor reviews a couple of books; the Notices also publishes longer submitted reviews of books of general interest, which include background material and a detailed description of the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer submitted reviews are typically 3–5 pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversation Articles — convert raw material to narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversation articles are either edited transcripts of interviews/panels or pieces that initiate a community conversation on a topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For interviews and panels, the author must use raw source material and turn it into a compelling narrative. Most conversation articles should be 3–5 pages and have at most a small number of references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tribute/Memorial Articles — focus, authorship, and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Memorial articles celebrate the lives, careers, and accomplishments of notable individuals; the primary aim is to tell a life story and inform readers about the person's contributions to the mathematical community and/or research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memorials should be 3–5 pages (rare exceptions by permission). They should be written by one or two primary authors responsible for gathering and organizing material from others. Include some pictures illustrating the person's life and work. Reminiscences and quotes are encouraged only if they serve a purpose and are not repetitive. Do not compile eulogies or personal reminiscences; avoid phrasing like 'X was a wonderful person' or 'I will miss X' — the focus must be on the person being memorialized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical Legacy companion articles
rubrics_metrics.description: For mathematicians whose work had far-reaching, long-lasting impacts, the Notices may consider publishing a companion article 'The Mathematical Legacy of X.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These companion articles should be 5–7 pages, with a significant portion accessible to a general mathematical audience. Authors should consult the editor-in-chief before proposing such an article; approval is limited by page budget.

rubrics_metrics.name: History Articles — audience, basis, and length
rubrics_metrics.description: History articles should interest a substantial proportion of Notices readers and may cover any period, area, or discipline. While not research articles, they should ideally be based on current or recent research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try to avoid technical language that is familiar to historians of mathematics but not standard terminology for the general mathematical community. Target length is 8–10 pages, with 15 pages as an absolute upper limit. Generally no more than 20 references unless justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Career Articles — topical breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: Career articles encompass all aspects of a mathematical career, including first-hand advice, reflections, and research about the mathematics profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative topics include how to write a good math article; navigating grants and fellowships; running a department; study tips for students; careers in industry/government; participating in the community; resources to help your career; incorporating LLMs into curriculum and research. (No single fixed length stated here; see related collections or consult editors.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters to the Editor — editorial discretion and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters to the Editor are generally not refereed, but the editor-in-chief reserves the right to negotiate changes with the author before publication and to reject material beyond the limits of normal professional discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect editorial negotiation and possible rejection for content deemed unprofessional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material published by the AMS Secretary — official communications
rubrics_metrics.description: The AMS Secretary uses the Notices to publish official communications from AMS leadership to members and the larger community, including calls for nominations, election results, biennial overviews, annual lists of prize winners, CEO statements, annual treasurer report, and similar items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Send such material to the AMS Secretary; these items follow the Secretary Collection practice in the Notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pictures in memorials
rubrics_metrics.description: Memorial articles should include some pictures that illustrate the person's life and work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pictures should support the life story and contributions; use them sparingly and purposefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permission and consultation for exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptions to stated limits (e.g., more references, longer page limits, special companion articles) require prior permission or consultation with the editor/ editor-in-chief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact the editor-in-chief or relevant Notices editor (email provided on the site) before submitting material that exceeds recommended lengths or reference counts; the Notices has a limited page budget so not all exceptions will be approved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical submission resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should use the Notices LaTeX style file and follow the Submission Page instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful links for authors (Notices Home Page, Submission Page, LaTeX style file, Collections) are provided on the page to make the authoring job easier.
